For a finite nonempty set identified with $[k]=\{1,\ldots,k\}$, a **probability vector** is $p=(p_i)_{i=1}^k$ with $p_i\ge0$ and $\sum_i p_i=1$; it is the outcome-weight vector of a finite probability space ([[def-finite-probability-space-and-event]]). Its Shannon entropy in natural units is
$$H(p):=-\sum_{i=1}^k p_i\ln p_i,$$
with $0\ln0:=0$. For probability vectors $p,q$ on the same set $[k]$, the relative entropy is
$$D(p\|q):=\sum_{i:p_i>0}p_i\ln(p_i/q_i),$$
with value $+\infty$ if $p_i>0=q_i$ for some $i$. A matrix $A\in[0,1]^{N\times m}$ is **row-stochastic** when each row sums to one. For a probability row vector $p$ on $[m]$ and a row vector $X\in[0,1]^m$, the dot product $pX^{\mathsf T}=\sum_{i=1}^m p_iX_i$ is the acceptance probability under distribution $p$.

These definitions use finite sets only; entropy is between $0$ and $\ln k$, as proved where needed below.

For $x>0$, define $\log x$ to be the unique real $y$ such that $\exp(y)=x$. This is well-defined because [[cor-exponential-is-a-bijection-onto-positive-reals]] states that $\exp:\mathbb R\to(0,\infty)$ is a bijection.

Thus $\log:(0,\infty)\to\mathbb R$ is the inverse function of $\exp$. In particular, $\log(\exp y)=y$ for every $y\in\mathbb R$ and $\exp(\log x)=x$ for every $x>0$.

The function $\log:(0,\infty)\to\mathbb R$ is continuous and strictly increasing, is onto $\mathbb R$, and satisfies, for $x,y>0$,
$$\log(xy)=\log x+\log y,\qquad \log(x/y)=\log x-\log y,\qquad \log(1/x)=-\log x.$$
Also $\log 1=0$.

finite-valued real- or complex-valued measurable representative in
$\mathcal L^1(\mu)$.  Then $A_nf$ converges $\mu$-almost everywhere to a
finite-valued integrable function $f^*$ satisfying

$$f^*\circ T=f^*\quad\mu\text{-almost everywhere},\qquad \lVert f^*\rVert_1\leq\lVert f\rVert_1.$$

The a.e. class of $f^*$ depends only on the a.e. class of $f$.  No ergodicity,
finite total measure, completeness, or invertibility is assumed.

Let $\mu(X)<\infty$, let $T$ preserve $\mu$, let $1\leq p<\infty$, and let
$f\in L^p(\mu)$ be real or complex valued.  If $f^*$ is its Birkhoff limit,
then $f^*\in L^p(\mu)$ and

$$\lVert A_nf-f^*\rVert_p\longrightarrow0.$$

No $L^\infty$ convergence is asserted.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be an arbitrary measure space. All functions below have domain $X$. Let $f$ and $(f_n)$ be measurable complex-valued functions such that

$f\in L^1(\mu)$,

For each measurable $E$, the Ces\`aro averages for $T^{-1}E$ and $E$ differ by $$\frac1N\sum_{j=0}^{N-1}P(T^{-(j+1)}E)-\frac1N\sum_{j=0}^{N-1}P(T^{-j}E)=\frac{P(T^{-N}E)-P(E)}N.$$ The numerator has absolute value at most $1$, so its quotient tends to zero. Taking limits, which exist by step 1.1 for both events, gives $\bar P(T^{-1}E)=\bar P(E)$. Thus the Ces\`aro limit is stationary in the sense of [F1].

The resulting law $\bar P$ is called the stationary mean when it is stationary in the sense of [F1]. If $E$ is strictly shift invariant, then each summand $P(T^{-j}E)=P(E)$; hence $P(E)=\bar P(E)$. Tail events are handled by the separate domination lemma, not by this invariant-event identity.

Call the AMS source ergodic when its stationary mean $\bar P$ is ergodic as a measure-preserving system under the same shift. This is a property of the mean, not a claim that $P$ itself is stationary.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

u$ be a signed measure on $(X,\mathcal A)$. Assume there is an increasing measurable exhaustion $(X_n)_{n\ge1}$ with $ igcup_n X_n=X$, $\mu(X_n)<+\infty$, and $|
u|(X_n)<+\infty$ for every $n$. Then there exist signed measures $
u_a,
u_s$ and a measurable real-valued function $f$ such that
$$
u=
u_a+
u_s,\qquad 
u_a\ll\mu,\qquad 
u_s\perp\mu,\qquad 
u_a(E)=\int_E f\,d\mu$$
for every measurable set $E$. The integral is always defined as an extended real number, and $\int_{X_n}|f|\,d\mu<\infty$ for every $n$.

measurable space $(X,\mathcal A)$. They are **mutually singular**, written
$$\mu\perp \nu,$$
when there are measurable sets $P,N\in\mathcal A$ with
$$P\cap N=\varnothing,\qquad P\cup N=X,$$
such that:

1. every measurable subset of $N$ has $\mu$-value $0$;
2. every measurable subset of $P$ has $\nu$-value $0$.

For positive measures this is equivalent to the usual condition
$\mu(N)=0$ and $\nu(P)=0$, because positivity turns vanishing on the ambient set
into vanishing on all measurable subsets.

u$ be a positive measure, a signed measure, or a complex measure on $(X,\mathcal A)$, and let $S\in\mathcal A$. We say that $

$$

Thus $c=O(n/\log n)$ and $|w|\le c=o(n)$.

Fix an information-lossless encoder $E$ with at most $s$ states. For each of the $c$ ordinary phrases $y_i$, record its starting state $S_i$, output word $W_i$, and ending state $S_{i+1}$. The tuples $(S_i,W_i,S_{i+1})$ are distinct: equality for two different phrase strings with the same initial state would contradict injectivity in [F3]. If $J$ is uniform on the $c$ phrases and $L=|W_J|$ has mean $\mu$, then $$\log_2c=H_2(S_J,W_J,S_{J+1})\le2\log_2s+H_2(L)+E L.$$ The two state entropies are at most $\log_2s$, by [F4] applied to the uniform law on each state set. Conditional on $L$, there are at most $2^L$ possible binary strings, so $H_2(W_J\mid L)\le E L$.

If $\mu=0$, then $H_2(L)=0$. If $\mu>0$, compare the finite-support law of $L$ with the geometric weights $r_j=(\mu+1)^{-1}(\mu/(\mu+1))^j$ restricted to that support. While text remains, let $w$ be the longest dictionary word prefixing the unread text, let $i$ be its dictionary index, and let $c$ be the next symbol. $H_n^{(2)}:=\mathbb E I_n^{(2)}(X_0^{n-1})=H_{\rm nat}(p_n)/\ln2.$
Finite summation and [[def-qa-35-finite-probability-entropy-and-stochastic-matrices]] show this equals $-\sum_{x:p_n(x)>0}p_n(x)\log_2p_n(x)$. For the Markov source, take stationary law $\pi=(1/2,1/2)$ and transition matrix $K$ with diagonal entries $3/4$ and off-diagonal entries $1/4$; direct multiplication gives $\pi K=\pi$. Its length-$n$ block probabilities are $$P(X_0^{n-1}=x_0^{n-1})=\tfrac12\prod_{i=1}^{n-1}K_{x_{i-1},x_i}.$$ Expanding the finite entropy sum with this factorization gives $$H_n=H(X_0)+\sum_{i=1}^{n-1}H(X_i\mid X_{i-1})=1+(n-1)H_2(1/4),$$ where $H_2(p)=-p\log_2p-(1-p)\log_2(1-p)$. $$L(x):=\int_1^x\frac{dt}{t},$$

using the oriented integral when $x<1$
([[def-oriented-integral]]).

This is well defined. The function $t\mapsto1/t$ is continuous wherever
$t\neq0$ by the quotient clause of
[[thm-algebra-of-continuous-functions]]. For $x\neq1$ it is therefore continuous on the nondegenerate compact interval
with endpoints $1$ and $x$, hence Riemann integrable there by
[[thm-continuous-implies-integrable]], whose hypothesis is $a<b$. At $x=1$ the
interval is degenerate and that theorem does not apply; there
[[def-oriented-integral]] stipulates $\int_1^1f=0$, so $L(1)=0$ directly.

For every $x>0$,

$$L(x)=\log x.$$

Let $a < b$ be reals and let $f, g : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be integrable
([[def-darboux-integral]]). Then:

1. **Nonnegativity.** If $f(x) \ge 0$ for every $x \in [a,b]$ then
   $\int_a^b f \ge 0$.
2. **Monotonicity.** If $f(x) \le g(x)$ for every $x \in [a,b]$ then
   $$\int_a^b f \;\le\; \int_a^b g .$$
3. **Two-sided bound.** If $m \le f(x) \le M$ for every $x \in [a,b]$, with
   $m, M$ real, then
   $$m\,(b-a) \;\le\; \int_a^b f \;\le\; M\,(b-a) .$$

function with integral $0$ may be positive at infinitely many points; that is
[[fs-nonnegative-integrable-with-zero-integral-vanishes]] on the previous page's
companion. Under the additional hypothesis of continuity the conclusion does
hold, and that is [[thm-nonnegative-continuous-with-zero-integral-vanishes]]
below.

convention of [[def-oriented-integral]], $f \le g$ gives
$\int_u^v f \le \int_u^v g$ when $u \le v$ and the reverse inequality when
$u \ge v$, since both sides change sign together.

For $x>0$, define $\log x$ to be the unique real $y$ such that $\exp(y)=x$. This is well-defined because [[cor-exponential-is-a-bijection-onto-positive-reals]] states that $\exp:\mathbb R\to(0,\infty)$ is a bijection.

Thus $\log:(0,\infty)\to\mathbb R$ is the inverse function of $\exp$. In particular, $\log(\exp y)=y$ for every $y\in\mathbb R$ and $\exp(\log x)=x$ for every $x>0$.

The function $\log:(0,\infty)\to\mathbb R$ is continuous and strictly increasing, is onto $\mathbb R$, and satisfies, for $x,y>0$,
$$\log(xy)=\log x+\log y,\qquad \log(x/y)=\log x-\log y,\qquad \log(1/x)=-\log x.$$
Also $\log 1=0$.

**Why this item is first.** The published definition of the integral does not
cover this page. [[def-darboux-integral]] is stated for reals $a < b$, because
the partitions it quantifies over are those of [[def-partition-and-refinement]],
whose standing hypothesis is $a < b$: with $a = b$ the chain
$a = t_0 < \dots < t_n = b$ is unsatisfiable. So $\int_a^b f$ is an undefined
symbol whenever $a \ge b$, and every additivity statement below would be
ill-formed as it is usually written. This item extends the notation, and nothing
else: the object it names is still the Darboux integral of
[[def-darboux-integral]].

Let $u, v \in \mathbb{R}$ and write

$$[u \wedge v,\ u \vee v] \;:=\; \text{the closed interval with endpoints } u \text{ and } v$$

([[def-interval]]). Let $f$ be a real-valued function whose domain contains that
interval. Say that **$f$ is integrable between $u$ and $v$** when either $u = v$,
or $u \ne v$ and the restriction of $f$ to $[u \wedge v,\ u \vee v]$ is bounded
([[def-bounded-set]]) and Darboux integrable there ([[def-darboux-integral]],
[[def-darboux-sums]]). For such $f$ define

$$\int_u^v f \;:=\; \begin{cases} \text{the Darboux integral of } f \text{ over } [u,v] & \text{if } u < v, \\[2pt] 0 & \text{if } u = v, \\[2pt] -\displaystyle\int_v^u f & \text{if } u > v. \end{cases}$$

**There is nothing to check for consistency.** The three clauses are indexed by
the three cases of trichotomy, $u < v$, $u = v$ and $u > v$, which are mutually
exclusive and exhaustive; no pair of them ever applies to the same $(u,v)$. In
particular the first clause is untouched, so on $u < v$ this is the published
integral verbatim and every published theorem about it applies unchanged.

**The middle clause is a stipulation, not a computation.** It is *not* claimed
that $0$ is a value forced by the $u < v$ definition in any limiting sense; that
definition simply says nothing at $u = v$, and $\int_u^u f := 0$ is what is
written there. It is also unconditional: no hypothesis on $f$ beyond being
defined at $u$ is asked for, since the case $u = v$ never refers to a partition.

### The two consequences used throughout the page

**Antisymmetry, for every pair.** For all reals $u, v$ with $f$ integrable
between them,

$$\int_u^v f \;=\; -\int_v^u f .$$

Indeed if $u < v$ then $v > u$ and the third clause reads
$\int_v^u f = -\int_u^v f$, which rearranges to the display; if $u = v$ both
sides are $0$; and if $u > v$ the third clause is the display itself.

**Absolute values agree.** Consequently
$\bigl|\int_u^v f\bigr| = \bigl|\int_v^u f\bigr|$ for every such pair.

**An obligation recorded here and discharged elsewhere.** With this convention
the additivity identity

$$\int_u^v f \;+\; \int_v^w f \;=\; \int_u^w f$$

holds for **every** arrangement of $u, v, w$ in an interval on which $f$ is
integrable, not only for $u < v < w$. That is a theorem and not part of this
definition; it is proved as the last clause of
[[thm-additivity-over-subintervals]], and nothing on this page uses it before it
is proved there.

For rational $0\le u<v\le1$, hold one unit after the martingale first falls to at most $u$, sell it when the martingale next reaches at least $v$, and repeat. Each finite-horizon gain is a sum of predictable holdings times martingale increments, so its expectation is zero by the martingale property. Every completed upcrossing earns at least $v-u$, and an unfinished holding loses at most one because the martingale stays in $[0,1]$. Thus the expected completed upcrossing count through any horizon is at most $(v-u)^{-1}$. The counts increase with the horizon, so [F4] gives finite expected total count and hence finitely many total upcrossings almost surely for each rational pair. A bounded real sequence that does not converge has distinct liminf and limsup, hence has infinitely many upcrossings of some rational interval strictly between them. A countable intersection over rational pairs, words and lengths therefore gives simultaneous almost-sure limits $q_{\infty,n}(w)$.

For each $n$, the limits are nonnegative and sum to one because there are finitely many words and every $q_{k,n}$ is a probability vector. They are $\mathcal F^-$-measurable. Every finite-past cylinder $B$ belongs to the conditioning sigma-algebra for all sufficiently large $k$; [F5], with majorant one on the probability space, then gives $\int_Bq_{\infty,n}(w)\,dP=P(B\cap\{X_0^{n-1}=w\})$.
